claim: The human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) US12 family consists of ten sequentially arranged genes (US12-21).
source: The human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) US12 family consists of ten sequentially arranged genes (US12-21) with poorly characterized function.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction of the manuscript.

claim: US12, US14, US18 and US20 have novel natural killer (NK) cell evasion functions.
source: We now identify novel natural killer (NK) cell evasion functions for four members: US12, US14, US18 and US20.
evidence: This claim is supported by NK cell degranulation assays shown in Figure 1B and described in the results.

claim: The US12 family selectively targets plasma membrane proteins.
source: we demonstrate that the US12 family selectively targets plasma membrane proteins and plays key roles in regulating NK ligands, adhesion molecules and cytokine receptors.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4, demonstrating preferential targeting of PM proteins.

claim: US18 and US20 work in concert to suppress cell surface expression of B7-H6.
source: US18 and US20 work in concert to suppress cell surface expression of the critical NKp30 ligand B7-H6 thus inhibiting NK cell activation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data (Figures 4C, 5A), flow cytometry (Figure 10), western blot (Figures 11D, 12A), and functional assays (Figures 12B-D, 13).

claim: The HCMV genome is 236 kb in size.
source: At 236 kb the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) genome is the largest of any characterized human virus and is comprised of long and short unique regions (UL and US), each flanked by inverted terminal repeats.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HCMV genome structure.

claim: HCMV codes for around 170 canonical protein-coding genes.
source: HCMV codes for around of 170 canonical protein-coding genes with 39 herpesvirus 'core' genes concentrated in the center of the UL region (Dolan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dolan et al., 2004.

claim: The majority of HCMV genes are not essential for virus replication in vitro.
source: The vast majority of the remaining HCMV genes are not essential for virus replication in vitro (Dunn et al., 2003) yet are replete with accessory functions, many of which have been implicated in suppressing host immune responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dunn et al., 2003.

claim: HCMV encodes 15 gene families of variable size.
source: Unusually, HCMV encodes 15 gene families of variable size that are often clustered on the genome (Davison et al., 2002; Holzerlandt et al., 2002; Chee et al., 1990; Dolan et al., 2004; Davison et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The US12 gene family consists of 10 genes arranged sequentially in the US region and transcribed in the same orientation.
source: The US12 gene family consists of 10 genes, designated US12 to US21, arranged sequentially in the US region and transcribed in the same orientation (Chee et al., 1990; Dolan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chee et al., 1990 and Dolan et al., 2004.

claim: The US12 family encodes 7-transmembrane spanning proteins with low-level homology to cellular TMBIM proteins.
source: The US12 family encodes a series of 7-transmembrane spanning proteins with low-level homology to the cellular transmembrane bax-inhibitor one motif-containing proteins (TMBIM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the US12 family structure.

claim: The US12 family is not essential for virus replication.
source: While not essential for virus replication, the US12 family has been implicated in HCMV tropism, virion maturation and immune evasion (Das and Pellett, 2007; Cavaletto et al., 2015; Bronzini et al., 2012; Hai et al., 2006; Gurczynski et al., 2014; Fielding et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NK cells play a critical role in controlling HCMV infections.
source: Natural Killer (NK) cells play a critical role in controlling HCMV infections, and the virus invests a substantial proportion of its coding capacity to inhibit NK cell activation (Wilkinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilkinson et al., 2013.

claim: US18 and US20 suppress cell surface expression of MICA.
source: We previously observed that US18 and US20 suppress cell surface expression of the NK cell-activating ligand MICA (Fielding et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fielding et al., 2014 and confirmed by data in Figure 10.

claim: The △US12-21 block deletion mutant induced substantially higher levels of NK cell degranulation compared to the parent HCMV.
source: In NK functional assays, the △US12-21 block deletion mutant induced substantially higher levels of NK cell degranulation compared to the parent HCMV with all four different donors tested (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B with data from four donors.

claim: Deletion of US12 resulted in significantly increased levels of NK activation in 3 of 4 donors.
source: Significantly increased levels of NK activation were detected in assays using deletion mutants of 5 different US12 family members: US12 (3 of 4 donors)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of US14 resulted in significantly increased levels of NK activation in 1 of 4 donors.
source: US14 (1 of 4 donors, with a trend towards increased NK activation in the other three donors)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of US18 resulted in significantly increased levels of NK activation in 3 of 4 donors.
source: US18 (3 of 4 donors)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of US20 resulted in significantly increased levels of NK activation in 4 of 4 donors.
source: US20 (4 of 4 donors)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of US21 resulted in significantly increased levels of NK activation in 4 of 4 donors.
source: US21 (4 of 4 donors) (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Three US12 family deletion mutants (US15, US16, US19) reduced the level of NK cell activation in some donors.
source: while three US12 family deletion mutants (US15, US16, US19) reduced the level of NK cell activation in some donors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The net effect of the complete US12 gene family is to inhibit NK cell recognition.
source: Although members of the US12 family are capable individually of either activating or suppressing NK cell function, the net effect of the complete US12 gene family is clearly to inhibit NK cell recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of individual deletion mutants versus the block deletion in Figure 1B.

claim: Mass spectrometry quantified 7215 WCL and 1281 PM proteins in Proteomic Series 1.
source: Mass spectrometry quantified 7215 WCL and 1281 PM proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Proteomic Series 1.

claim: The impact of the US12 family was most noticeably focused on the plasma membrane.
source: The impact was most noticeably focused on the PM, in that the majority of WCL proteins affected were also PM 'hits' (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 comparing PM and WCL proteomes.

claim: The US12 family regulates protein expression or stability of cell surface proteins.
source: For a given PM protein modulated by the US12 gene family (Figure 4), comparable results were observed in WCL samples (Figure 5), suggesting that the US12 family regulates protein expression or stability of cell surface proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing PM and WCL data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Multiple KEGG pathways were significantly enriched among proteins rescued by the US12-21 deletion.
source: Multiple KEGG pathways were significantly enriched (data not shown), including natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity (MICA, MICB, ULBP2, IFNGR1), cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (IL6ST, KIT, KITLG, ACVRL1, ACVR1, IFNGR1) and cell adhesion molecules (CAMs; JAM3, ICOSLG, PTPRM, MPZL1, CXADR, ALCAM, SDC4, CD99, SDC1).
evidence: This is based on DAVID pathway analysis of proteomic data.

claim: B7-H6 was regulated by the US12-21 mutant but not identified by DAVID analysis.
source: A further NK ligand, B7-H6, was not identified by DAVID analysis, but was also regulated by the US12-21 mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in proteomic data (Figures 4C, 5A).

claim: The regulation of B7H6, MICB and ULBP2 by the US12 family are novel findings.
source: While MICA is a recognized target of US18 and US20 (Fielding et al., 2014), the regulation of the NK cell activating ligands B7H6, MICB and ULBP2 by the US12 family are novel.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by proteomic and validation data.

claim: A substantial subset of proteins regulated by the US12-21 block mutant were similarly modulated by US18 and US20.
source: A substantial subset of the proteins regulated by the US12-21 block mutant were similarly modulated by US18 and US20 (Figure 4, Figure 5)
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: US19 specifically targeted RALGPS2.
source: whereas US19 specifically targeted RALGPS2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mass spectrometry quantified 7156 whole cell and 1312 PM proteins in Proteomic Series 2.
source: Mass spectrometry quantified 7156 whole cell and 1312 PM proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Proteomic Series 2.

claim: The majority of target proteins were regulated by both US18 and US20.
source: A striking feature of this data was that the majority of these target proteins were regulated by both US18 and US20, with a subset additionally regulated to a lesser degree by US14 and/or US16 (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: US12 and US13 mutants regulated the NKG2D ligands ULBP2 and MICB respectively.
source: Other US12 family members also had important effects, with US12 and US13 mutants regulating the NKG2D ligands (NKG2DL) ULBP2 and MICB respectively
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: US14 mutant regulated PTPRM.
source: US14 mutant regulating PTPRM
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: US15 mutant regulated IL6ST.
source: and the US15 mutant regulating IL6ST (Figure 4C–E and Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4C-E and Figure 6.

claim: The contribution made by a given US12 family member varied dramatically from one cellular target (US13 and US19) to 54 cellular targets (US20).
source: Overall, the contribution made by a given family member varied dramatically ranging from the highly focused impact of US13 and US19 (one cellular target each) to the exceptionally promiscuous US20 (54 cellular targets) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: MICA was regulated by the deletion of US12-21 block to a much greater extent than any of the single deletion mutants.
source: Interestingly, MICA was regulated by the deletion of US12-21 block to a much greater extent than any of the single deletion mutants, implying that multiple US12 family members may need to act in concert to optimize control over certain cellular targets (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Infection with the US21 deletion mutant resulted in selective impairment of many late phase Tp3 and Tp5 HCMV proteins.
source: Infection with the US21 deletion mutant resulted in selective impairment of many late phase Tp3 and Tp5 (Temporal protein profile 3 and 5) HCMV proteins (Weekes et al., 2014), for example UL32 and UL99/pp28, and elevated expression of pUS20
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citation to Weekes et al., 2014.

claim: The HCMV US12-21 block mutant did not recapitulate the effect on late phase viral proteins observed with the US21 deletion mutant.
source: whereas the HCMV US12-21 block mutant did not recapitulate this effect (Figure 7, with further proteomic data searchable in Excel spreadsheet Supplemental file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Deletion of the US21 structural gene impacts on the transcriptional control of US20.
source: Our data are consistent with deletion of the US21 structural gene impacting on the transcriptional control of US20 (data not shown), and may contribute to a potential growth defect observed for this particular mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing elevated pUS20 expression in the US21 deletion mutant.

claim: The activation of NK cells in response to US21 mutant-infected targets cannot be assigned directly to an effect of US21.
source: Therefore the activation of NK cells in response to US21 mutant-infected targets cannot be assigned directly to an effect of US21 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that US21 deletion affects US20 expression.

claim: The majority of proteins that the US12 family down regulates from the PM are also lost from the WCL.
source: The majority of proteins that the US12 family down regulates from the PM are also lost from the WCL, consistent with post-translational proteolysis or an overall reduction in expression.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing PM and WCL proteomic data.

claim: US20 targets MICA for degradation in lysosomes.
source: We previously found that US20 targets the NKG2DL MICA for degradation in lysosomes (Fielding et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fielding et al., 2014.

claim: DAVID pathway analysis identified increases in lysosomal proteins within the PM fraction of △US20-infected cells.
source: The DAVID pathway analysis identified increases in lysosomal proteins within the PM fraction of △US20-infected cells; the list of lysosomal proteins included a number of cathepsins and ATPases (PSAP, CTSD, ATP6V1E1, ATP6V1H, NPC2) (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on DAVID pathway analysis of proteomic data.

claim: US20 plays a role in regulating intracellular endo-lysosomal vesicular transport.
source: These data suggest a role for US20 in regulating intracellular endo-lysosomal vesicular transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing lysosomal protein changes.

claim: The △US12-21 'block' deletion caused substantial shifts in WCL proteins, with >80 proteins rescued >2 fold at 48 hr.
source: The △US12-21 'block' deletion caused substantial shifts in WCL proteins, with >80 proteins rescued >2 fold at 48 hr, compared to the parent viral infection (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B from Proteomic Series 3.

claim: 26% of proteins rescued by the US12-21 deletion were also rescued >2 fold with leupeptin.
source: Of these, 26% were also rescued >2 fold and 51% > 1.5 fold with leupeptin suggesting that the US12 family targets multiple host proteins to the lysosome.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: Leupeptin treatment had a more limited effect on rescuing PM proteins back to the cell surface.
source: Leupeptin treatment had a more limited effect on rescuing PM proteins back to the the cell surface (Figure 8B), consistent with our previous observation of intracellular accumulation of MICA without protein relocalisation to the cell surface during treatment with leupeptin or other lysosomal inhibitors (Fielding et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and supported by citation to Fielding et al., 2014.

claim: 11 of 21 key proteins in categories 'natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity', 'cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction' and 'cell adhesion molecules' were rescued >2 fold by leupeptin.
source: Of the 21 proteins identified in Figure 4 within the key categories 'natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity', 'cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction' and 'cell adhesion molecules', 11 were rescued >2 fold by leupeptin, with the remainder exhibiting 1.3–2-fold rescue (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C.

claim: MICB was clearly rescued by leupeptin treatment.
source: MICB was clearly rescued by leupeptin treatment (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Control of MICB and ULBP2 levels correlated with regulation of UL16 by US13 and US12.
source: Interestingly, control of MICB and ULBP2 levels correlated with regulation of UL16 by US13 and US12 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9.

claim: Many cellular substrates of the US12 family are being targeted for lysosomal degradation.
source: Although many cellular substrates of the US12 family are clearly being targeted for lysosomal degradation, there may be additional mechanisms by which this family regulates the PM proteome.
evidence: This is inferred from the leupeptin rescue experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Flow cytometry validated a proportion of the PM protein targets regulated by the US12 family.
source: We used flow cytometry to validate a proportion of the various PM protein targets that are regulated by the US12 family (Figure 10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10.

claim: MICA expression was rescued to a greater degree with the US12-21 block mutant than with the individual US18 or US20 deletion mutants.
source: We found that MICA expression was rescued to a greater degree with the US12-21 block mutant than with the individual US18 or 20 deletion mutants (Figure 10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10.

claim: A combined US18 and US20 deletion had a greater effect on cell surface MICA than single gene deletion mutants.
source: This is consistent with our previous analysis showing that a combined US18 and US20 deletion had a greater effect on cell surface MICA than single gene deletion mutants (Fielding et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fielding et al., 2014.

claim: The US13 deletion mutant caused a minor, but consistent, elevation in cell surface expression of MICB.
source: The US13 deletion mutant caused a minor, but consistent, elevation in cell surface expression of MICB.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10.

claim: There was a further increase in MICB expression in the US12-21 block mutant compared to US13 deletion alone.
source: Other US12 family genes may yet contribute to regulating MICB, as there was a further increase in the US12-21 block mutant (Figures 10 and 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 10 and 4C.

claim: B7-H6 is the major ligand identified for the natural cytotoxicity receptor NKp30.
source: B7-H6 is the major ligand identified for the natural cytotoxicity receptor (NCR) NKp30 and a tumor antigen (Brandt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brandt et al., 2009.

claim: B7-H6 expression was shown to be induced by inflammatory stimuli.
source: Previously, B7-H6 expression was shown to be induced by inflammatory stimuli, for example pro-inflammatory cytokines and bacterial-derived toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands (Matta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matta et al., 2013.

claim: B7-H6 expression is induced as a stress protein by HCMV infection.
source: We show here that B7-H6 expression is induced as a stress protein by HCMV infection (and potentially other virus infections)
evidence: This is shown in proteomic data (Figures 4C, 5A), flow cytometry (Figure 10), and western blot (Figure 12A).

claim: Exogenous expression of B7-H6 in fibroblasts increased NK degranulation.
source: B7-H6 is a known ligand for NKp30 and exogenous expression in fibroblasts increased NK degranulation (Figure 11A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11A-C.

claim: Ectopic expression of US20, and to a lesser extent US18, reduced levels of exogenously expressed B7-H6.
source: Ectopic expression of US20, and to a lesser extent US18, from adenovirus vectors reduced levels of exogenously expressed B7-H6 detected by immunoblotting (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11D.

claim: Both PM and WCL expression of B7-H6 was induced by the HCMV US18, US20 and US12-21 deletion mutants but not by the parental virus.
source: Both PM and WCL expression of B7-H6 was induced by the HCMV US18, US20 and US12-21 deletion mutants but not by the parental virus (Figure 4C, Figure 5A), which was confirmed by flow cytometry and immunoblot (Figures 10 and 12A).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4C, 5A, 10, and 12A.

claim: US18 and US20 act in concert to target B7-H6 for proteolysis.
source: B7-H6 is therefore induced as a 'stress ligand' during productive infection, but its expression is controlled by US18 and US20, acting in concert, to target it for proteolysis (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C and supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The presence of US18 and US20 was required to inhibit NKp30 reporter activity.
source: We investigated the effect of the US12 family members upon activation of an NKp30-responsive reporter cell line, and found that the presence of US18 and US20 was required to inhibit reporter activity (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Reporter cell fluorescence could be inhibited by transfection of B7-H6 specific siRNA.
source: Reporter cell fluorescence could be inhibited either by transfection of B7-H6 specific siRNA or by use of a B7-H6 specific blocking antibody (CH31) (Figure 12C and D respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Reporter cell fluorescence could be inhibited by use of a B7-H6 specific blocking antibody.
source: Reporter cell fluorescence could be inhibited either by transfection of B7-H6 specific siRNA or by use of a B7-H6 specific blocking antibody (CH31) (Figure 12C and D respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12D.

claim: B7-H6 knockdown in cells infected with HCMV US18 and US20 deletion mutants reduced donor NK cell activation.
source: B7-H6 knockdown in cells infected with HCMV US18 and US20 deletion mutants was correspondingly able to reduce donor NK cell activation (Figure 13A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 13A and B.

claim: The impact of B7-H6 knockdown on the HCMV US12-21 block mutant was more variable.
source: The impact of B7-H6 knockdown on the HCMV US12-21 block mutant was more variable and consistent with the US12 gene family encoding additional NK modulating functions (Figure 13B, Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 13B and inferred from Figure 1.

claim: A B7-H6 blocking antibody reduced NK activation in response to the US18, US20 and US12-21 deletion mutants to levels of the parental HCMV control.
source: A B7-H6 blocking antibody had an even more pronounced effect, reducing NK activation in response to the US18, US20 and US12-21 deletion mutants to levels of the parental HCMV control (Figure 13C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 13C.

claim: B7-H6 plays a major role in NK cell recognition of HCMV-infected cells.
source: These results are consistent with B7-H6 playing a major role in NK cell recognition of HCMV-infected cells, a function that is countered by the US12 family members US18 and US20.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data in Figures 12 and 13.

claim: Clusters of US12-related genes can be detected in cytomegaloviruses of New World primates.
source: Clusters of US12-related genes can be detected in cytomegaloviruses of New World primates, i.e. Green Monkey and Owl Monkey CMVs, thus the capture and expansion of an ancestral precursor presumably took place over 41 million years ago (Davison et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davison et al., 2013.

claim: Within Cynomolgus and Rhesus macaques, chimpanzee and human CMVs, the US12 family is maintained as a well conserved contiguous tandem array of 10–11 genes.
source: Within Cynomolgus and Rhesus macaques (Old World primates), chimpanzee and human CMVs, the US12 family is maintained as a well conserved contiguous tandem array of 10–11 genes located in the same relative position on each genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CMV evolution.

claim: The US12 family exhibits relatively high levels of sequence conservation and genetic integrity amongst circulating HCMV clinical strains.
source: Amongst circulating HCMV clinical strains, the US12 family exhibits relatively high levels of sequence conservation and genetic integrity (Sijmons et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sijmons et al., 2015.

claim: The US12 family targets T-cell co-stimulatory molecules, cell adhesion molecules, and cytokine/cytokine receptors.
source: By systematically analyzing a bespoke panel of HCMV deletion mutants, we have discovered that the US12 family selectively targets a broad range of plasma membrane proteins that include, not only NK cell activating ligands, but also T-cell co-stimulatory molecules, cell adhesion molecules, and cytokine/cytokine receptors.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Figures 2-6.

claim: A sizeable proportion of targeted plasma membrane proteins are degraded in lysosomes.
source: A sizeable proportion of targeted plasma membrane proteins do not accumulate internally, but are degraded in lysosomes, as indicated by rescue with the inhibitor leupeptin.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: The overlap between US12 gene family targets and KSHV K5 viral E3 ubiquitin ligase targets could represent convergent evolution.
source: The overlap that exists between US12 gene family targets with those of the KSHV K5 viral E3 ubiquitin ligase (MICA, MICB, B7 family, ALCAM, IFNGR1, PTPRM, EPHA2, CD99, MPZL1/2) could represent convergent evolution and/or targeting of similar cellular pathways (Timms et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with published data, supported by citation to Timms et al., 2013.

claim: The NKG2DL MICB and ULBP2 are strongly upregulated during HCMV infection.
source: The NKG2DL MICB and ULBP2 are strongly upregulated during HCMV infection, but fail to reach the cell surface as they are retained in the ER by the NK evasion function gpUL16 (Rolle et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rolle et al., 2003.

claim: Deletion of US12, US13 and US20 leads to increased cell surface and intracellular expression of MICB, ULBP2 and UL16.
source: Our proteomic data reveal that deletion of US12, US13 and US20 leads to increased cell surface and intracellular expression of MICB, ULBP2 and UL16 itself (Figure 9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9.

claim: US12 family members act in concert to direct UL16, MICB and ULBP2 towards proteolytic degradation.
source: These observations are consistent with US12 family members acting in concert to direct UL16, MICB and ULBP2 towards proteolytic degradation, with leupeptin treatment clearly able to rescue MICB, and this may contribute to the NK evasion properties of US12 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data in Figures 8 and 9, and NK functional data in Figure 1.

claim: Some effects of the US12 family could be the result of co-operation with other HCMV genes.
source: They also imply that some of the effects of the US12 family could be the result of co-operation with other HCMV genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of US12 family effects on UL16.

claim: Co-operation between US2 and UL141 was observed in the proteasomal degradation of CD112.
source: There is some precedent for this situation, although not previously on such a wide scale, as co-operation between US2 and UL141 was observed in the proteasomal degradation of some protein targets e.g. CD112 (Hsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2015.

claim: None of the US14 targets are recognized NK cell ligands.
source: None of the US14 targets are recognized NK cell ligands, suggesting that this gene product utilizes a novel NK evasion mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data and NK functional assays.

claim: NKp30 is expressed on γδ T-cells (Vδ2-) that are induced during HCMV infection post-transplantation.
source: The control of B7-H6 is likely to be of major significance as NKp30 is expressed on γδ T-cells (Vδ2-) that are induced during HCMV infection post-transplantation and correlate with control of disease (Merville et al., 2000; Lafarge et al., 2001; Correia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merville et al., 2000; Lafarge et al., 2001; Correia et al., 2011.

claim: Many adhesion molecules play roles in co-stimulation or immune synapse formation of T-cells.
source: Many of these adhesion molecules play roles in co-stimulation or immune synapse formation of T-cells e.g. ALCAM, ICOSLG, CXADR (Hassan et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2000; Witherden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hassan et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2000; Witherden et al., 2010.

claim: The US12 family targets pro-inflammatory mediators including multiple members of the TNFR superfamily.
source: The US12 family targets pro-inflammatory mediators, such as multiple members of the tumour necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) superfamily (TNFRSF8, TNFRSF12A, NGFR, LTBR), gp130 (IL6ST), the IL-6 receptor signaling receptor, pannexin-1 (PANX1) and the TLR4 ligand high-mobility group protein B1 (HMGB1) (Croft et al., 2013; Kanneganti et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data and citations to Croft et al., 2013; Kanneganti et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004.

claim: IL6ST signaling may have antiviral effects in the context of HCMV.
source: IL6ST signaling may also have antiviral effects in the context of HCMV (Harwardt et al., 2016), which was suggested by the finding that disruption of gp130 STAT3 binding resulted in IFN-like signaling through STAT1(Costa-Pereira et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harwardt et al., 2016 and Costa-Pereira et al., 2002.

claim: The closest cellular homologues to the US12 family are the TMBIM family.
source: The closest cellular homologues to the US12 family are the TMBIM family with recognised functions in controlling apoptosis, ER stress, ROS production, actin production, glucose metabolism and protein trafficking (Rojas-Rivera and Hetz, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rojas-Rivera and Hetz, 2015.

claim: The US12 family may have arisen through an 'accordion' gene expansion from a 'captured' ancestor TMBIM gene.
source: The US12 family may have arisen through an 'accordion' gene expansion from a 'captured' ancestor TMBIM gene.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on homology to TMBIM family.

claim: US21 displays the highest level of homology with TMBIM1/4 among the US12 family.
source: Out of the entire US12 family, US21 displays the highest level of homology with TMBIM1/4, with the homologous region limited to the transmembrane domain and loops (unpublished observations, [Lesniewski et al., 2006; Holzerlandt et al., 2002]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lesniewski et al., 2006 and Holzerlandt et al., 2002.

claim: TMBIM family have cytosolic N- and C-termini with six full transmembrane spanning regions.
source: The divergence of the US12 and TMBIM families is also reflected in their different membrane topologies, as TMBIM family have cytosolic N- and C-termini with six full transmembrane spanning regions, and US20 has a cytosolic N-terminus and lumenal C-terminus (Carrara et al., 2012; Cavaletto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carrara et al., 2012 and Cavaletto et al., 2015.

claim: US20 has a cytosolic N-terminus and lumenal C-terminus.
source: The divergence of the US12 and TMBIM families is also reflected in their different membrane topologies, as TMBIM family have cytosolic N- and C-termini with six full transmembrane spanning regions, and US20 has a cytosolic N-terminus and lumenal C-terminus (Carrara et al., 2012; Cavaletto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carrara et al., 2012 and Cavaletto et al., 2015.

claim: A number of TMBIMs target proteins for lysosomal degradation.
source: The functional relevance of the US12 family/TMBIM homology remains unclear, although it may represent a 'functional scaffold' (Lesniewski et al., 2006), as a number of TMBIMs also target proteins for lysosomal degradation (Lee et al., 2012; Yamaji et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lesniewski et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2012; Yamaji et al., 2010.

claim: The US12 family targets multiple host immune ligands consistent with having arisen through immune selection.
source: Our data indicate that the US12 family targets multiple host immune ligands, consistent with the family having arisen, been selected and diverged in function as a consequence of immune selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive proteomic and functional data presented.

claim: US12 family genes differ from the majority of characterised immune evasion viral genes in that they act together and do not exhibit single gene effects.
source: US12 family genes differ from the majority of characterised immune evasion viral genes, as they act together and do not exhibit single gene effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing overlapping targets among family members.

claim: The targeting of multiple proteins by a HCMV immunevasin or co-operation between HCMV gene products was not previously observed on this scale.
source: The targeting of multiple proteins by a HCMV immunevasin or co-operation between HCMV gene products is not unprecedented, but was not previously observed on this scale or with this diversity of target proteins (Tomasec et al., 2005; Prod'homme et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomasec et al., 2005; Prod'homme et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of US12 family targets contain an immunoglobulin-like domain.
source: The majority of US12 family targets contain an immunoglobulin-like domain, including the MHC I-related proteins, MICA and B7-H6.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of the target proteins identified in the proteomic data.

claim: The US12 family is a critical region for regulation of the host immune response.
source: Our data highlight the importance that HCMV gene families are likely to play in terms of HCMV persistence in vivo and identifies the US12 family as a critical region for regulation of the host immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive functional and proteomic data presented.

claim: Of all PM proteins regulated >3 fold by a member of the US12-21 family, 29% were regulated by 2 or more family members.
source: Of all PM proteins regulated >3 fold by a member of the US12-21 family, 29% were regulated by 2 or more family members and 6% by 3 or more family members (Figure 6)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: 6% of PM proteins regulated >3 fold by a member of the US12-21 family were regulated by 3 or more family members.
source: Of all PM proteins regulated >3 fold by a member of the US12-21 family, 29% were regulated by 2 or more family members and 6% by 3 or more family members (Figure 6)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-regulation of proteins by multiple US12 family members may suggest evolutionary pressure underpins the expansion of this gene family.
source: Such co-regulation may suggest evolutionary pressure underpins the expansion of this gene family.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed co-regulation patterns.
